analysis.one_liner: Bars payday and high-interest lenders from collecting debts for one year from borrowers hit by COVID-19.
analysis.headline: A one-year ban on debt collection by payday and high-cost lenders against pandemic-affected borrowers was introduced in April 2020, drew no cosponsors, never left the House Financial Services Committee, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped payday lenders, auto title lenders, and other non-bank lenders charging 36% interest or more from collecting on loans made to borrowers affected by COVID-19. Affected borrowers could notify a lender that they had lost income, become unemployed, or been hospitalized due to the pandemic, and the lender would then be barred for one year from calling, texting, contacting employers, tapping bank accounts, sending accounts to collection agencies, or reporting missed payments to credit bureaus. It also covered any loan where the lender never checked whether the borrower could afford the payments while covering basic living expenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers with payday, auto title, or other high-cost loans whose income, job, or health was hit by COVID-19. They would get a year of relief from collection calls, bank account withdrawals, employer contact, collections lawsuits, and damage to their credit reports. The trigger is broad: anyone living or working in a federally, state, or locally declared emergency area qualifies, which covered most of the country during the pandemic.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Strapped borrowers with payday or high-cost loans

how_it_helps.text: For one year after a borrower notifies a lender they were affected by COVID-19, the lender cannot carry out any collection efforts on covered loans.

Covered loans include any loan with a nominal interest rate of 36% or more, and any loan from a covered lender that did not check whether the borrower could afford payments while meeting basic living expenses.

Collection efforts are defined to include phone calls and texts, contacting the borrower's employer, cashing post-dated checks or withdrawing from bank accounts, turning debts over to collection agencies, and reporting missed payments to credit bureaus.
A borrower qualifies as affected by COVID-19 if household income fell, they lost a job, a household member was hospitalized, or they live or work in a declared emergency area.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, auto title lenders, and other non-bank high-cost lenders, who would lose a year of collections on loans to pandemic-affected borrowers, plus the collection agencies and credit bureaus that work with them. Borrowers would still owe the money after the year ends; the bill pauses collections rather than canceling the debt.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium pauses collections but does not forgive the debt: after the one-year period ends, lenders could resume every collection effort, leaving borrowers to face the full balance plus accrued amounts later.

A broad, unqualified one-year collection ban could push some lenders to stop making loans to borrowers in hard-hit areas altogether, cutting off credit for people with no other options during an emergency.
Borrowers must notify the lender that they are affected to trigger protection, and the burden of that process falls on people already dealing with lost income or illness.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers drowning in 400% APR payday loans during a national emergency, a year without bank account seizures, employer calls, and credit damage would have been meaningful breathing room. The design is modest and temporary: it does not cap rates permanently, does not cancel debt, and requires borrowers to invoke it themselves. Critics would fairly note that blocking all collections without a repayment plan could reduce credit availability. On balance the bill's benefits go directly to financially distressed households at the expense of a small group of high-cost lenders.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2020, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gregory Meeks introduced the bill on April 17, 2020, roughly a month into the COVID-19 pandemic and economic shutdown.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and that referral was the last action ever taken on it.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday and other high-cost lenders kept collecting on pandemic-affected borrowers without interruption, since no moratorium was ever enacted. Borrowers in distress got no federal collection relief from this bill.

for.name: Gregory Meeks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Payday and Predatory Loans Moratorium Act of 2020 and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or consideration during the remainder of the 116th Congress.

against.name: Payday lending industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed pandemic-era restrictions on payday collection and lending, and the bill's committee never advanced any version of them.

sides.party_line_note: A single House Democrat sponsored the bill and no Republican or additional Democratic member cosponsored it; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: These lenders profit from loans at 36% interest and above, often due in full within a month, and the bill would have barred them from collecting on loans to pandemic-affected borrowers for a year. Their revenue depends on aggressive collection, including bank account withdrawals and post-dated check cashing, which the bill names directly.

industries.industry: Non-bank installment and high-cost consumer lenders
industries.note: Any non-depository lender that did not verify a borrower's ability to afford payments while covering basic living expenses would be covered by the collection ban. The bill would have made unaffordable lending unenforceable for a year.
The bill prohibits covered lenders from entering agreements with collection agencies on these debts during the moratorium, cutting off a stream of referred accounts.
The bill bans reporting missed payments on covered loans to credit bureaus during the moratorium, temporarily reducing the flow of derogatory consumer data they sell.
